stem: Under the AICPA Code's definitions, which of the following is confidential client information?

choices.text: Any information obtained from the client that is not available to the public; unless particular client information is available to the public, it is considered confidential.
Only information the client has marked confidential in writing.
Any information about the client, including what the client has published on its own public website.
Only the client's financial information; a client's name alone can never be confidential client information.

feedback: The Code's definition is any information obtained from the client that is not available to the public, and its interpretation sets the default: unless the particular client information is available to the public, it should be considered confidential client information. Choice (b) adds a marking requirement that appears nowhere in the definition. Choice (c) contradicts the Code's own list of what is available to the public, which includes publicly accessible websites, databases, online discussion forums, and other electronic media. Choice (d) contradicts the Code's example: where a practice is limited to bankruptcy matters, disclosing a client's name could suggest financial difficulties and may itself be confidential client information. Re-read section 01.

No flag inherited.

stem: Before disclosing confidential client information to a third-party service provider, what does the AICPA Code's interpretation give as the member's two options?

choices.text: Enter into a contractual agreement with the provider to maintain confidentiality and obtain reasonable assurance that the provider has appropriate procedures in place, or obtain the client's specific consent before the disclosure.
Notify the client after the disclosure has been made, or obtain the provider's verbal promise of confidentiality.
Either option is waived when the provider is a widely used company; the Code exempts well-known vendors.
Obtain the client's general consent to the firm's use of outside help, without naming the information, the type of third party, or its intended use.

feedback: The interpretation's first route is a contractual agreement with the third-party service provider to maintain the confidentiality of the information plus reasonable assurance that the provider has appropriate procedures in place; the other is specific consent from the client before disclosing. Choice (b) puts the client's involvement after the disclosure and substitutes a verbal promise for the contract the Code names. Choice (c) invents an exemption; the Code says only that how much assurance work is needed depends on factors including the extent of publicly available information on the provider's controls. Choice (d) describes consent that is not specific: the Code says consent should specify the nature of the information, the type of third party, and its intended use. Re-read section 02.
_source: drafts/GPT-source-index.md file 1 entry 8 (contract plus reasonable assurance) and entry 10 (specific consent before the disclosure); entry 9 (publicly available information on the provider's controls as a factor) and entry 11 (what consent must specify) for the distractors; guide/07/02-third-party-service-providers.md, "The first route" and "The second route". No flag inherited.

stem: Under New Hampshire RSA 309-B:18 as this lesson presents it, what is the one general release from a licensee's duty not to voluntarily disclose information communicated by the client?

choices.text: Permission of the client for whom the licensee performs services, or of the client's heirs, successors, or personal representatives.
A confidentiality contract with the recipient plus reasonable assurance about the recipient's procedures.
The recipient's status as a third-party service provider engaged by the licensee.
Written notice to the state board before the disclosure.

feedback: The section opens with its release: except by permission of the client for whom a licensee performs services, or the heirs, successors, or personal representatives of such client. Its remaining exceptions are specific cases the chapter does not prohibit: disclosures required by the profession's reporting standards, disclosures under subpoena or summons, licensing and ethics investigations and peer review, need-to-know sharing inside the organization serving the client, and quality control. Choice (b) is the AICPA Code's first route for third-party service providers; the statute's exceptions contain no such clause. Choice (c) names a category the section does not mention. Choice (d) describes a procedure that appears nowhere in the section. Re-read section 03.
_source: drafts/GPT-source-index.md file 5 entry 2 (permission of the client) and entries 5–9 (the exceptions); file 5 "Does not cover" (no service-provider, vendor or contractor clause) and file 1 entry 8 (the Code's contract route) for distractor (b); guide/07/03-new-hampshire-rsa-309-b-18.md, "What the statute says" and "What is not on the list". No flag inherited.

stem: What does the AICPA Code's authoritative text itself say about a member's use of AI?

choices.text: It does not name ChatGPT, a language model, or generative AI; it notes, by reference, that a nonauthoritative staff article discusses threats to compliance with the Code when members use AI to provide services, and it does not reproduce that article.
It defines entering client information into a chatbot as a disclosure of confidential client information.
It names AI vendors as third-party service providers and lists the assurance a member must obtain from them.
It prohibits members in public practice from using generative AI to provide professional services.

feedback: The Code's authoritative text never names ChatGPT, a language model, or generative AI. What it says about AI is a note that a nonauthoritative article, "Ethics Staff Insights: AI through an ethics lens", discusses threats to compliance with the Code when members use AI to provide services; the Code does not reproduce it. Choice (b) attributes to the Code the position section 04 states as this course's own. Choice (c) attributes to the Code an application it does not make; whether a model vendor is a third-party service provider is a question the Code does not answer. Choice (d) states a prohibition the Code does not contain. Re-read section 04.
_source: drafts/GPT-source-index.md file 1 entry 18 (the Code's reference to the staff article on AI) and file 1 "Does not cover" (the Code never names ChatGPT, an LLM, or generative AI in authoritative text; applying 0.400.52 and 1.700.040 to a model vendor is the author's inference); guide/07/04-this-courses-position.md, first paragraph. The section's three flagged sentences are the course's position; no choice's correctness depends on it, and distractor (b) is wrong precisely because it puts the position in the Code's mouth.

stem: What does the CPA.com Generative AI Toolkit give as its general rule on client information and public tools, and what does it say to do with personal information before it enters any AI tool?

choices.text: As a general rule, no client or business information is entered into a public LLM; personal information is de-identified, or sanitized, before it is ingested into both internal AI systems and public tools.
Client information may be entered into a public LLM once the user has turned the training setting off.
De-identification is required only for public tools; internal AI systems are exempt because the firm controls them.
The rule is limited to confidential client information; client information that is not confidential under the Code may be entered freely.

feedback: The toolkit's general rule is that no client or business information should be entered into a public LLM, and its policy term is that the policy should prohibit uploading or asking questions about client data within a public generative AI tool; its security practice is to de-identify (sanitize) personal information before ingesting it into both internal AI systems and public tools. Choice (b) links the toolkit's rule to a training setting; the toolkit names no setting and no plan, and lesson 2's pages say nothing about the toolkit's rule. Choice (c) drops the toolkit's own words, which include internal systems. Choice (d) narrows the toolkit's scope; its sentence says client or business information, not confidential client information. Re-read section 05.
_source: drafts/GPT-source-index.md file 4 entry 12 (no client or business information into a public LLM), entry 11 (the policy prohibits client data in a public generative AI tool) and entry 13 (de-identify before ingesting into internal and public tools); file 4 "Does not cover" (no ChatGPT setting, plan or data control) for distractor (b); guide/07/05-keeping-client-data-out.md, "The general rule" and "Before anything is uploaded". The section's one flagged sentence (reading an individual plan as a public tool) is not what any choice turns on.

stem: According to the CPA.com toolkit, what should happen before a client's confidential information is shared with a third party vendor, including AI?

choices.text: Written disclosure to the client and the client's specific consent, in the appropriate format, before the confidential information is shared.
Nothing further, provided the firm's engagement letter mentions that the firm uses AI.
Verbal notice to the client after the information has been shared.
The vendor's confirmation that it does not train on the firm's data.

feedback: The toolkit's sentence is: if a client's confidential information will be shared with a third party vendor, including AI, provide written disclosure to and obtain specific consent from the client in the appropriate format before the confidential information is shared. Choice (b) confuses that practice with a separate one: the toolkit says to consider disclosing a firm's use of AI in the engagement letter even when disclosure is not specifically required, and does not say the letter replaces consent. Choice (c) is neither written nor before. Choice (d) describes a vendor commitment lesson 2 covered; nothing in the toolkit makes it a substitute for the client's consent. Re-read section 06.
_source: drafts/GPT-source-index.md file 4 entry 14 (written disclosure and specific consent before sharing with a third party vendor, including AI); entry 15 (consider disclosing AI use in the engagement letter) for distractor (b); guide/07/06-consent-disclosure-and-the-policy.md, "Disclosure and consent". No flag inherited.

stem: A member's practice is limited to bankruptcy matters. A software vendor asks the member for a list of the firm's clients so that it can tailor a demonstration. Under the AICPA Code as this lesson presents it, which statement is accurate?

choices.text: The client names may be confidential client information, because in a practice limited to bankruptcy matters disclosing a client's name could suggest that the client is experiencing financial difficulties; unless the information is available to the public, the Code says to consider it confidential.
Names are never confidential client information, because the Code's definition is limited to financial data.
The names are confidential only if the clients have asked the firm in writing to keep them confidential.
The names are available to the public because the firm itself is publicly listed, so the Rule does not reach them.

feedback: The Code's own example is a practice limited to bankruptcy matters, where disclosure of the client's name could suggest that the client may be experiencing financial difficulties, which may be confidential client information; and its interpretation says that unless particular client information is available to the public, it should be considered confidential. Choice (b) narrows the definition, which is any information obtained from the client that is not available to the public. Choice (c) adds a request requirement the definition does not contain. Choice (d) confuses the firm's public existence with the client information's availability; the Code's test is whether the particular information is available to the public, on publicly accessible websites, databases, forums, or other electronic media. Re-read section 01.
_source: drafts/GPT-source-index.md file 1 entry 5 (the bankruptcy-practice example), entry 4 (the default), entry 2 (the definition) and entry 3 (available to the public); guide/07/01-the-confidential-client-information-rule.md, "What is confidential", "The default" and "A client's name". The scenario is hypothetical, names no client and states no fact (GPT-05 review J3). No flag inherited.

stem: A member is considering a third-party service provider and has read the provider's published description of its security controls. Which statement matches the AICPA Code's interpretation as this lesson presents it?

choices.text: The extent of publicly available information on the provider's controls is one factor in how much work reasonable assurance takes; the member still needs a contractual agreement with the provider to maintain confidentiality, or else the client's specific consent, and must be able to demonstrate that safeguards were applied.
Published controls are themselves reasonable assurance, and nothing further is required of the member.
Once the provider is engaged, responsibility for the confidentiality of the information passes to the provider.
The client's specific consent is required in addition to the contract; the Code offers no route to a provider without the client's consent.

feedback: The Code's interpretation says that how much assurance work is needed depends on factors including the extent of publicly available information on the provider's controls and procedures; that the first route is a contractual agreement to maintain confidentiality plus reasonable assurance about the provider's procedures, and the other is the client's specific consent; and that a member is in violation if the member cannot demonstrate that safeguards were applied that eliminated or reduced significant threats to an acceptable level. Choice (b) turns one factor in the assurance assessment into the whole of it and drops the contract. Choice (c) contradicts the demonstration sentence and the General Standards Rule's interpretation, under which the member must also obtain sufficient relevant data to support the work product. Choice (d) misstates the interpretation, which gives the contract-and-assurance route as an alternative to consent, not a companion to it. Re-read section 02.
_source: drafts/GPT-source-index.md file 1 entry 9 (publicly available information as a factor), entry 8 (contract plus reasonable assurance), entry 10 (specific consent as the other route), entry 12 (violation if safeguards cannot be demonstrated) and entry 16 (the member still obtains the data); guide/07/02-third-party-service-providers.md, "The first route", "The second route" and "What stays with the member". The scenario names no provider and states no fact (GPT-05 review J3). No flag inherited.

stem: A licensee in New Hampshire is comparing RSA 309-B:18 with the AICPA Code's interpretation on third-party service providers. Which comparison matches this lesson?

choices.text: The Code's interpretation allows disclosure to a provider under a confidentiality contract with reasonable assurance, or with the client's specific consent; the statute's exceptions contain no service-provider clause and its only general release is the client's permission, so the state rule is the narrower of the two, and the Code itself says to consider whether state law is more restrictive.
The statute incorporates the Code's interpretation by reference, so the two rules are the same for a New Hampshire licensee.
The statute lists the same exceptions as the Code, including a clause for third-party service providers under contract.
The Code overrides the statute for AICPA members, so a member in New Hampshire may rely on the Code's contract route alone.

feedback: The Code's interpretation gives two routes, a contractual agreement with reasonable assurance or the client's specific consent, and says the member should consider whether federal, state, or local statutes concerning the confidentiality of client information may be more restrictive; the statute's release is permission of the client, and its exceptions name reporting standards, legal process, investigations and peer review, need-to-know sharing inside the organization serving the client, and quality control, with no service-provider clause. Choice (b) invents an incorporation the section does not contain. Choice (c) puts the Code's clause into the statute's list. Choice (d) reverses the Code's own direction to consider more restrictive state law. Re-read sections 02 and 03.
_source: drafts/GPT-source-index.md file 1 entry 13 (consider whether state law is more restrictive), entry 8 and entry 10 (the Code's two routes); file 5 entry 2 (permission of the client), entries 5–9 (the exceptions) and file 5 "Does not cover" (no service-provider clause); the index Gaps ("the two rules do not line up"); guide/07/03-new-hampshire-rsa-309-b-18.md, "What is not on the list". The correct choice compares the two texts and does not rest on section 04's position. No flag inherited.

stem: A firm is writing its policy on the use of ChatGPT. Which set of practices is the CPA.com Generative AI Toolkit's, as this lesson presents it?

choices.text: No client or business information into a public LLM; de-identify personal information before it enters any AI tool, internal or public; written disclosure to and specific consent from the client before confidential information is shared with a third party vendor, including AI; consider disclosing the firm's AI use in the engagement letter; and define ordinary versus extraordinary use, with producing professional advice as extraordinary.
Client data may be entered into any tool, provided a human verifies the response before it is used.
De-identification replaces the need for consent, so a firm that sanitizes data before upload need not tell the client.
All AI use must be reported to the state board of accountancy in advance.

feedback: Those are the toolkit's sentences: no client or business information into a public LLM; de-identify (sanitize) personal information before ingesting it into both internal AI systems and public tools; provide written disclosure to and obtain specific consent from the client before confidential information is shared with a third party vendor, including AI; consider disclosing a firm's use of AI in the engagement letter even if not specifically required; and define ordinary use, such as writing marketing language, versus extraordinary use, such as using AI to produce counsel or professional advice. Choice (b) substitutes lesson 4's review practice for the toolkit's rule on what goes in; the toolkit states both, and neither replaces the other. Choice (c) joins two practices the toolkit states separately and makes one waive the other, which the toolkit does not say. Choice (d) describes a requirement that appears in none of this lesson's sources. Re-read sections 05 and 06.
